title: Haloalkanes & haloarenes
examples: What is the difference between SN1 and SN2 reactions?
How does the structure of the halogen affect reactivity?
Can elimination happen if a good leaving group is present?

explain.say: Today we will look at haloalkanes and haloarenes.
First we look at nucleophilic substitution reactions.
The SN2 mechanism occurs in a single step.
The SN1 mechanism involves a carbocation intermediate.
Next we examine elimination reactions, like E2.
In reality, the reaction conditions determine the main product.

faq.q: What is the main difference between SN1 and SN2?
faq.a: SN2 is a single, concerted step where the nucleophile attacks at the same time the leaving group departs. SN1 is a two-step process involving a planar carbocation intermediate.
asks: How many steps are in SN1 versus SN2?
Does SN2 happen all at once?

faq.a: Haloarenes are much less reactive than haloalkanes because the benzene ring stabilizes the carbon-halogen bond. They usually require harsh conditions to react.

faq.q: When do I favor elimination over substitution?
faq.a: You favor elimination when you use a strong base, as bases are better at removing a proton than nucleophiles are at attacking a carbon.
asks: How do I make an alkene instead of a substituted product?

faq.q: Does the structure affect the reaction pathway?
faq.a: Yes, primary substrates favor SN2, while tertiary substrates favor SN1 due to stability of the carbocation.
asks: Does structure matter for SN reactions?

faq.q: What is a good leaving group?
faq.a: A good leaving group is one that forms a stable anion when it departs, such as bromide or chloride ions.
asks: What makes a good leaving group?
Which halogens are good leaving groups?

facts: SN2 reactions are favored by strong nucleophiles and primary substrates.
SN1 reactions are favored by weak nucleophiles and tertiary substrates.
Elimination reactions are favored by strong bases, promoting alkene formation.
Haloarenes are less reactive than haloalkanes due to resonance stabilization.

quiz.say: Predict the major product when tert-butyl bromide reacts with hydroxide ion.
quiz.why: Tertiary substrates strongly favor the carbocation formation pathway, leading to elimination.

wrong.1: This is tempting because hydroxide is a nucleophile, but the tertiary structure favors elimination.
wrong.2: SN2 reactions are disfavored by tertiary substrates due to steric hindrance.
wrong.3: While carbocations form, the base is strong enough to promote elimination over rearrangement.

quiz.say: Which reaction mechanism is favored by a primary haloalkane and a strong nucleophile?
quiz.why: Primary substrates and strong nucleophiles strongly favor the backside attack mechanism.

wrong.1: SN1 requires a stable carbocation, which is difficult to form from primary substrates.
wrong.2: While E2 is possible, the high nucleophilicity makes substitution the more likely primary pathway.
wrong.3: E1 is a two-step process that is less favored than the direct SN2 pathway here.

quiz.say: If we treat 2-bromo-propane with sodium ethoxide, what is the expected major product?
quiz.why: Ethoxide is both a strong base and a good nucleophile, favoring the elimination (E2) pathway.

wrong.0: This suggests SN2, but the strong base pushes the reaction toward elimination.
wrong.1: This suggests SN1, which is less favored than the concerted E2 mechanism under these conditions.
wrong.3: This assumes substitution is favored, ignoring the strong basic nature of ethoxide.
